evidence.note: ruling recorded under the retired format
tree over files, hashes recorded per file
digest width per leaf

Q077.resolution: A per-file hash is BLAKE3 over the file bytes exactly. The path is the leaf's label in the Merkle tree, not part of the hashed content, so renaming a file changes the tree without pretending the bytes changed.
Q077.text: Is a per-file hash over bytes or bytes plus path?

evidence.note: metadata-only packages are legal
an empty payload still has a hash

Q078.resolution: Empty files are legal leaves; an empty payload is legal and its root is the BLAKE3 of the empty input under the domain tag. A metadata-only package already establishes that a package may carry no content.
Q078.text: Are empty files and empty payloads legal?

evidence.note: the determinism rule the walk follows
what is being ordered

Q079.resolution: The walk is ordered by path byte order, not manifest order, because canonical serialization already sorts keys by byte order and the tree must be reproducible by a second writer.
Q079.text: Is the walk ordered by path bytes or manifest order?

evidence.note: files are the leaves
layout changes are versioned

Q080.resolution: The walk covers files only. Directories are implied by the paths in the tree and are not leaves, so an empty directory is not representable, consistent with a payload that carries content rather than filesystem metadata.
Q080.text: Does the walk include directory entries?

evidence.note: the signed statement's contents
the hash's scope, which embedding makes circular

Q081.resolution: The signature is detached, never embedded. The signed statement binds name, revision and hash, and the hash covers the canonical package bytes; an embedded signature would sit inside the bytes it covers.

evidence.note: the scheme in use
the envelope shape being reused

Q082.resolution: Ed25519, carried in the family's dl-enclave.sig/1 envelope. It is the scheme the existing store and checkpoints already use, so Restore reuses one signature scheme rather than introducing a second.

evidence.note: the payload root lives in the manifest
the manifest is the preimage's core

Q083.resolution: The envelope covers the canonical manifest only. The payload root is a field of that manifest, so the payload is covered transitively and a payload substitution changes the verified bytes.
Q083.text: Does the envelope cover the manifest only or also the payload root?

evidence.note: the signed field set
identity is stable across promotion

Q084.resolution: No timestamp is inside the signed bytes. The signature binds name, revision and hash; a signed timestamp would make a re-sign change identity and contradict a promoted prerelease keeping its hash.
Q084.text: Is a timestamp inside the signed bytes?

evidence.note: re-signing creates coexisting signatures
each signature binds the same statement

Q085.resolution: Multiple signatures are allowed and ordered. Rotation is per release and every stored package is re-signed at rotation, so a package can carry an outgoing and an incoming signature during a transition.

evidence.note: the existing envelope field
rotation makes key selection necessary

Q086.resolution: The envelope carries a key identifier. The family's existing envelope already carries key-id, and per-release rotation makes discovery by trial unsafe.
Q086.text: Does the envelope carry a key identifier?

evidence.note: Ed25519 keys are generated on the first checkpoint, checkpoint.key (0600) and checkpoint.pub — one pair, no history
the dl-enclave.sig/1 envelope carries key-id, but nothing consults it
case-insensitive 'revok' has zero occurrences; no revocation, expiry or key_history representation exists

Q087.resolution: Revocation is not represented. The store holds one generated Ed25519 checkpoint key pair with no key history and no expiry, and the signature envelope's `key-id` is carried but never consulted. Replacing the key file retires nothing retroactively.
Q087.text: Is revocation represented in the store?

evidence.note: no key history, no expiry today
the statement a past key covers

Q088.resolution: A key that signed while valid keeps verifying its own signatures. The store has no expiry representation today, and when Restore adds key history the check is trust-at-signing plus current revocation, not current validity.
Q088.text: Does an expired key still verify old signatures?

evidence.note: Q010 already fixed rotation per release; Q089 restates it

Q089.text: One key per release or per package?

evidence.note: the manifest is inside the hash
what the envelope binds

Q090.resolution: Beside the manifest, not inside it. Same circularity as Q081: the manifest is what the hash covers, so a signature stored inside it would cover itself.
Q090.text: Is the signature stored inside or beside the manifest?

evidence.note: the revision is outside identity
content identity is the package bytes

Q091.resolution: No new revision. The revision is not part of the BLAKE3 preimage and the hash covers the package alone, so adding a signature changes neither identity nor content; the event is recorded in the ledger and the store's envelope set, not in the revision number.
Q091.text: May a signature be added after publish without a revision?

evidence.note: the versioned envelope carries its own schema
revision is bound inside, not the envelope's version

Q092.resolution: The envelope schema is versioned separately from the package revision. The family already names the envelope dl-enclave.sig/1, which is its own version, and a package revision move does not renumber it.

evidence.note: the workspace refusal rule
what is being verified

Q093.resolution: A failed signature is a refusal, by name. The workspace rule is refuse-never-default, and the shell's security boundary refuses a package that cannot prove identity rather than mounting it with a warning.
Q093.text: Is a failed signature a refusal or a warning?

Q102.resolution: No. A stream schema bump does not bump the mount receipt schema, and a receipt bump does not disturb the stream.

evidence.note: order is a stated property

Q103.resolution: Chunks carry an explicit sequence and are applied in order. A gap, a duplicate or a reordering is a truncation-class refusal, never a silent resort.

evidence.note: resume is stated as authenticated
unverified bytes are never adopted

Q104.resolution: Resume is authenticated. The resuming side re-presents the package identity, and a resume without a verifiable signature is refused rather than trusted.

evidence.note: the property is stated
the family's existing rule

Q105.resolution: Operation ids make delivery idempotent: a retried chunk or apply carrying the same operation id takes effect once, and the second arrival is acknowledged without a second effect.
Q105.text: Are operation ids idempotent, and what does a retry do?

evidence.note: detection is a stated property
the consequence

Q106.resolution: Truncation is detected against the declared size and the digest, not against the transport closing. The refusal is `stream-truncated`.

evidence.note: explicit, not implied
the failure it prevents

Q107.resolution: Finalization is explicit: the stream ends with a finalization record. An EOF without one is a truncation, not a short but acceptable stream.
Q107.text: Is finalization explicit or implied by EOF?

evidence.note: the property is stated
what holds until the switch

Q108.resolution: Adoption is atomic: the mounted surface switches in one step, so a partially applied revision is never visible.

evidence.note: the full gate list

Q109.resolution: Only after digest, signature, schema, compatibility and client-surface checks all pass, in that order.
Q109.text: When may the client drop the previous admitted revision?

evidence.note: refusal, not conversion
the behaviour already asserted in the family

Q110.resolution: No conversion on read. The frame is refused by name with `found` and `supported`, which the family's own reader already does and its own test asserts.
Q110.text: Are older or newer frames converted on read?

evidence.note: the streamer's own identity
the stream tag is separate from package identity

Q111.resolution: Yes. The streamer is itself a package with its own identity, separate from the packages it carries, so a streamer revision never renumbers its payload packages.
Q111.text: Does the stream carry its own package identity?

evidence.note: what the stream carries

Q112.resolution: The manifest travels inline in the canonical package bytes. The chunk manifest is the stream's own framing and is not a second copy of the package manifest.
Q112.text: Does the manifest travel inline or separately?

evidence.note: the existing ceiling
boundedness is a stated property

Q113.resolution: A chunk is bounded and the bound is declared per frame. The family's arrival frame already caps a payload at 1 MiB, and Restore adopts that ceiling rather than inventing a second number.

evidence.note: the subordination rule

Q114.resolution: Yes, and it rides as a subordinate contract with its own version, so a stream change does not renumber receipts.
Q114.text: Does the receipt ride the stream?

evidence.note: what a receipt means
mount-and-render witness is the required proof

Q115.resolution: The client. It is a witness that the surface mounted and rendered, not the server's assertion that bytes were sent.

evidence.note: the refusal
the classification

Q116.resolution: The mount is indeterminate, not successful: refusal `receipt-mismatch`, and the previous revision stays.
Q116.text: What if the receipt names a different revision than the mount?

evidence.note: the recorded failure this prevents
identity excludes framing

Q117.resolution: No. Encryption is transport; the digest is over canonical content, and re-framing or re-encrypting the same content must not move it.
Q117.text: Does transport encryption affect package identity?

evidence.note: nothing partial becomes visible
a bad prefix is a truncation-class failure

Q118.resolution: Yes. The digest covers the whole content, so a resumed assembly re-verifies the prefix before finalization and adopts nothing on trust.
Q118.text: Does a resumed stream re-verify the prefix?

evidence.note: the existing refusal
the same refusal in Restore's failure model

Q119.resolution: `frame-schema`, carrying `found` and `supported`. The family's ingest reader already refuses that way.
Q119.text: What refusal names an unsupported frame?

evidence.note: the recorded rule
the mechanism that replaces negotiation

Q120.resolution: No. The frame names its schema and the reader refuses what it does not support; there is no negotiation and no downgrade.

evidence.note: the receipt contract owns its version
where the receipts already live

Q121.resolution: The mount receipt is `surface.mount/2`. It keeps its own version and its own reader, and it lives in the family's existing mount store (`dl-enclave` `MountStore`).
Q121.text: What is the mount receipt's own schema tag?

evidence.note: the non-coupling rule
the receipt's own axis

Q122.resolution: No. A stream schema bump does not bump the mount receipt schema, and a receipt bump does not disturb the stream.
Q122.text: Does the receipt schema move with the stream schema?

evidence.note: closed, not open
the field that does not exist

Q123.resolution: Closed. A receipt carries a closed state set plus a separate refusal code, and there is no warnings field.
Q123.text: Is the receipt state set closed or open?

evidence.note: degraded is a state
and carries a refusal code

Q124.resolution: A state. `degraded` enters the state set and must name its cause in `refusal`; it is non-applied, so the applied-row and floor logic already exclude it.
Q124.text: Is `degraded` a state or a warning?

evidence.note: the receipt's producer
the witness's producer

Q125.resolution: The client. The mount row of the signing table assigns the adopted revision to a client receipt, and the witness row assigns rendering to the client.

evidence.note: the separation
where authorization actually lives

Q126.resolution: No. A receipt is evidence of adoption, not authorization to adopt; admission is a server-policy verdict recorded separately.
Q126.text: Is a receipt authorization to adopt?

evidence.note: subject plus digest
what a mismatch is called

Q127.resolution: The revision actually adopted: the receipt identity is a subject and its digest, and a receipt naming a different revision than the mount is `receipt-mismatch`.

evidence.note: the row names the receipt
the row is the record

Q128.resolution: The ledger row is the durable record; the mount receipt is the subject that row names. The chain, its fsync and its append-only file are the durability, and the receipt is what the row points at.
Q128.text: Is the receipt the durable record, or is the ledger row?

evidence.note: the refusal for an unseen check
what does not count as a witness

Q129.resolution: No. A check the client cannot see is `test-surface-unwitnessed`, and a check that runs only in Node, a headless browser or a separate witness page is not a witness.
Q129.text: Can a receipt be produced without rendering?

evidence.note: the ruling that both are required
the rendering half

Q130.resolution: No. Both are required: the mount-and-render witness and the parity digest. The digest proves the bytes arrived; the witness proves the surface rendered.
Q130.text: Is a parity digest alone sufficient as a witness?

evidence.note: a withdrawn revision still resolves
rows are not rewritten

Q131.resolution: They remain, and the pin still resolves: a withdrawn revision stays retired forever but still resolves for the consumer that pinned it.
Q131.text: What happens to receipts when a revision is withdrawn?

evidence.note: the append-only invariant
how removal is recorded

Q132.resolution: No. Ledger rows are never deleted or edited; retention removes encrypted vault blobs and appends a `retention` entry naming what it removed.

evidence.note: the record rule
the negative form

Q133.resolution: Yes, when it is a ledger entry: the ledger entry is the durable record of the witness, and a check that did not write an entry did not run.
Q133.text: Does a receipt count as completion evidence for a ticket?

evidence.note: what a checkpoint does not do
the checkpoint contract in code

Q134.resolution: Not individually. Authenticity comes from the chained ledger: a checkpoint signs a head that is in the chain, and a checkpoint does not prove the truth of the entries it covers.

evidence.note: the condition
how it is reported

Q135.resolution: Absent is a reported state, never a passing receipt: a health check that never ran is reported as absent and never as a pass.
Q135.text: Does an `absent` receipt exist, or is absent the absence of a receipt?

evidence.note: the receipt store
the ledger's relationship to it

Q136.resolution: No. Receipts live in the mount store (`dl-enclave` `MountStore`); the ledger row names the receipt as its subject. Two stores, one authority each.
Q136.text: Is the receipt store the same store as the ledger?

evidence.note: verbatim: Kept forever; receipts and their evidence are never removed

Q137.resolution: Retention never removes a mount receipt or the evidence it points at. The retention action covers encrypted vault blobs of conversation text only; no receipt is ever named in a retention row.
Q137.text: How long are mount receipts retained before the retention action removes them?

evidence.note: verbatim: Publishable in full, including evidence refs

Q138.resolution: Receipts may leave the machine in full, evidence refs included. There is no redaction projection and no withheld field.
Q138.text: May mount receipts leave the machine — published, exported or shared outside it?

Q139.resolution: All three, in order: a recorded workday of cadence ticks, then the 24-hour continuous simulation, then a count of independently verified tasks. A day passes only when all three hold.
